findings.rationale: Observed outcome prevalence (~0.58) is far above what the client's features imply (mean predicted ~0.21). CITL is strongly negative (about -0.37 at round 20) and negative from round 1 onward, with a large ECE. AUC is only modestly lower (0.785), so discrimination is intact. Symmetric label flipping cannot produce this prevalence from a ~0.21 base, so the fault is a prevalence shift. Update norm is high (median ratio 4.66) and cosine to the median is negative, which is consistent with training on wrong-prevalence data rather than poisoning. Subgroup O/E in the Sex attribute is elevated in both groups, with no low-O/E under-diagnosis pattern.

Observed prevalence (~0.55) is more than double the feature-implied rate (mean predicted ~0.23). CITL is about -0.32 and negative across most rounds, with a very high ECE. AUC is normal (0.850), so the labels' intercept is shifted while the feature ranking is preserved. Update norm is anomalous (median ratio 5.67) with a negative mean cosine. Subgroup outcomes are elevated across Sex and several income groups, which points to prevalence rather than subgroup under-recording.

Observed prevalence (~0.50) is far above the feature-implied rate (mean predicted ~0.22), with CITL of about -0.28 and a high ECE. AUC is normal to high (0.871), so discrimination is intact and the fault is a prevalence/intercept shift rather than label noise. Update norm is elevated (median ratio 3.49) with a negative mean cosine. Confidence is lower because the client is small (n_train 723), so its per-round values are noisy, and it has a weak Sex-feature drift flag (z=3.7) that is not confirmed across rounds.

report.summary: Screened all 52 clients with client_updates, client_performance, drift_by_round, feature_summary, and subgroup_outcomes (Sex, AgeGroup, Income), then confirmed leads with narrower queries and attribution_churn. Three clients (KS, ME, MT) show a consistent prevalence shift: observed outcome prevalence is roughly double or more what their features imply, CITL is strongly negative from round 1, and discrimination (AUC) is normal or near-normal. Symmetric label flipping cannot reproduce these prevalences, so I classified them as prevalence_shift, with onset round 1. Their update norms are elevated with negative cosines, but this is explained by their data faults, not poisoning, since their local performance is abnormal. Leads I dismissed as noise: CT and ND feature-tail outliers (not reproduced on re-query), CA's age-group-8 O/E outlier (overall CA performance normal, z_noise ~3), and small-client drift and subgroup flags (DC, MT drift; GU, VI, GA, CT, WY, DC, NH subgroup rows) that are below the confirmation threshold. No poisoning, free-rider, or explanation-instability signature was found: attribution churn decreases smoothly, consistent with normal convergence. No subgroup_bias pattern (no low-O/E under-recording). Budget: about 19.5 of 20 spent."
